PAPER: QUESTIONNAIRES APPLICATION Published Online: November 19, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multirev.2026282 From reviews to revenue: The power of electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) and brand image in shaping consumer purchase intentions Bhawana Kotharia | Ambica Prakash Mania aDepartment of Commerce, Graphic Era (Deemed to Be University), Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India. Abstract This research examines the impact of electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) on consumer purchase intention (PI) while also analyzing the mediating effect of brand image (BI). This study examines how online comments (eWOM) affect young buyers’ purchase intentions while considering environmental aspects, as this study focused on the users of herbal cosmetics products. The data were collected from 482 online consumers through a Google questionnaire, which was shared online and offline. Structural modeling was performed with SmartPLS software. This research demonstrates that eWOM significantly positively impacts purchase intention, with a partial mediation effect that is played by brand image. These innovative findings lay the groundwork for developing a better and clearer understanding of the online behavior of consumers and have important implications for marketers regarding the management of eWOM and BI control. Finally, the research outlines its limitations and proposes future research directions that explore pathways for a more in-depth exploration of eWOM dynamics and their impact on the decision-making of consumers within the digital marketplace context. Keywords: herbal cosmetics, brand image (BI), consumer behavior, purchas intention (PI), electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) 1. Introduction The swift progress of digital technologies and the widespread use of social networking sites have transformed consumer buying behavior, especially with respect to information-gathering and decision-making processes. Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) has become a significant determinant of consumer purchase intentions (PIs), facilitating the sharing and access of product-related information beyond conventional marketing channels (Cheung & Thadani, 2012). eWOM includes all negative or positive information about products being generated and shared by consumers through digital channels. It has a growing role in determining how a brand is perceived, which in turn affects consumer purchases (Hussain et al., 2018). Its growing importance has driven many companies, particularly in the cosmetic industry, to employ eWOM strategies to increase brand engagement and drive sales (Simamora, 2023). The herbal cosmetic industry has experienced notable growth attributed to heightened consumer awareness of natural and organic beauty products (Babić Rosario et al., 2020). There is an increasing consumer preference for herbal and ayurvedic cosmetics, driven by concerns regarding synthetic chemicals and their possible adverse effects (Ali & Raza, 2017). BI functions as a crucial intervening variable in the connection between eWOM and PI. Previous studies have shown that favorable eWOM reinforces BI, subsequently increasing consumer trust and the likelihood of buying behavior in cosmetic products or services (Kim & Ko, 2012; Jalilvand & Samiei, 2012). A robust brand enhances emotional and cognitive ties with consumers, thereby increasing the persuasive effectiveness of eWOM messages (Zhang et al., 2020). Despite extensive studies on the relationship between eWOM and PI across various industries, few studies have focused on the dynamics within the herbal cosmetics sector, especially in the Indian marketplace. This study investigates the digital marketplace in depth. It aims to equip businesses with valuable insights into leveraging eWOM. By examining BI, we uncover strategies to increase marketing efforts. Our findings highlight eWOM's crucial role in shaping brand perceptions. This research seeks to address an existing research gap by offering marketers and industry practitioners insights into how to optimize digital communication strategies and improve the position of a brand in the marketplace in the context of the herbal cosmetics market. In this digital age, eWOM is the unsung hero of marketing success. 1.1. Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) is the process through which information about one or several topics is shared through digital channels. Compared with conventional or long-established word-of-mouth, eWOM is more widely distributed, Multidiscip. Rev. Past studies have demonstrated that eWOM strongly influences consumer decision-making, brand perception, and purchasing behaviors. eWOM refers to consumers publishing their experiences, opinions, or recommendations of products, services, or brands via digital networks, which typically include brand websites and online stores. These include information available on social media, comments made on digital platforms, activities within forums, and other forms of digital communication that influence consumer decisions and can change their likelihood of purchasing a product. As computer-mediated communications grow, eWOM provides a way for consumers to engage in noncommercial communication, where real-life experiences about a specific product or brand are shared, exchanged, and discussed (Chevalier & Mayzlin 2006). eWOM is a beneficial source of information, as it offers details on brand experiences that cannot be found in the sources controlled by organizations. It is expected that consumers will consider a brand for consumption when they see positive eWOM communication about the product or brand (Park & Lee, 2008). Therefore, we can see that customers appreciate eWOM as a key informational source, irrespective of whether it is favorable or unfavorable, in shaping the PI of customers toward a brand (Kim et al., 2014). 1.2. Brand image (BI) Brand image is the painting created by customer attitudes and beliefs. It stitches together thoughts and feelings into a textured tapestry of connections. This powerful mosaic has a critical effect on how customers engage and behave toward a brand. Strong brand imagery inspires and uplifts loyal customers, increasing their perceived value. This drives higher purchase intent. BI is also described by (Keller, 1993; Severi & Ling, 2013) as consumer sentiment and beliefs about a brand. BI is a mental representation of a brand and its uniqueness in comparison to other brands in the market (Lee et al., 2011). Therefore, the correct BI may have an effect on consumer PI. BI leaves an everlasting impression on consumers, resulting in a feeling of importance and emotional connection with them. 1.3. Purchase intention (PI) Purchase intention is a window into how likely a consumer is to buy. The PI can also be said of as online buying intent or intent to buy online. It serves as a reliable compass guiding the actual purchasing decisions of consumers (Wu & Wang, 2011). Various factors shape this intention, including individual attitudes and prevailing social norms. External influences, such as marketing messages, peer recommendations, or online website comments, also play their part. Together, these elements weave a complex tapestry of consumer behavior. According to (Pavlou, 2003), customers’ intention to purchase online, whether through an online shop or brochure, is their willingness to purchase. An online purchase intent refers to when a buyer decides to complete a purchase in an e-web store, that is, if a buyer has considered all relevant factors before making a purchase and now has made up his or her mind to purchase the product. According to (Farzin & Fattahi, 2018), online buying intent is said to be the consumer’s disposition to obtain a product. 1.4. Connection between eWOM, BI and PI Previous studies have indicated that eWOM can substantially influence PI. Favorable eWOM is effective in improving and enhancing PI, leading to a relatively high propensity to buy it, whereas unfavorable eWOM yields adverse effects (Zahid & Endang Ruswanti, 2024). However, the exact nature of these relationships in which BI plays a mediating role in the relationship between eWOM and PI requires further investigation in response to herbal cosmetics consumption. (Cheung et al., 2008) discovered that favorable online reviews, which include positive evaluations and recommendations, enhance the image of a company by creating trust and credibility. This is accomplished via good online reviews and comments. This, in turn, increases the likelihood that clients would consider the organization to be trustworthy and of high quality. eWOM, which comprises digital platform recommendations, online reviews, social media posts, and comments, has been documented to have a direct and favorable impact on the PI. The connection between eWOM and PI has been documented in multiple studies. The development of eWOM over products has consistently been associated with consumers’ purchase intentions, given its ability to deliver credible and contextual information to consumers. One of many studies researching cosmetic products has shown that favorable online reviews and recommendations can increase consumers’ confidence in making purchase decisions and, in many cases, also change their purchase decisions rather than being confused or doubtful (Vithana & Fernando, 2024; Saputra & Jatra, 2024; Simamora, 2023). The relationship between eWOM and the PI depends critically on the BI. The studies reveal that eWOM impacts the BI, which in turn shapes purchase intention. Positive eWOM enhances consumers’ perceptions of a brand, making it more favorable and trustworthy. For example, a study on herbal cosmetic products revealed that online reviews and social media discussions significantly improved BI, which subsequently influenced purchase decisions. For example, a study on Avoskin https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Kothari and Mani (2026) 3 products demonstrated that eWOM positively influences BI, which in turn increases PI (Supradita et al., 2020; Indriana et al., 2022). Some studies suggest that BI intercedes the connection, indicating that eWOM also has a direct effect on PI alongside its indirect effect through BI (Arifah et al., 2024; Kusuma et al., 2022). A hedonic BI is a perception, emotion, or meaning that consumers construct from abstract and imagery-related factors that are not necessarily connected to brand quality, performance, or utility (Gensler et al., 2013). Hypotheses and Conceptual Model Development On the basis of the previous literature, the following hypotheses are proposed (Figure 1): • H1: Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) has a significant influence on consumer purchase intention (PI). • H2: Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) has a significant influence on brand image (BI). • H3: Brand image (BI) has a significant influence on consumer purchase intention (PI). • H4: Brand image (BI) mediates the relationship between electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) and consumer purchase intention (PI). 3. Methodology 3.1. Sampling and data collection To test the proposed hypothesis, this study employed a quantitative research design. This research employed nonprobability sampling techniques, as the sample selection was aligned with the study’s primary objective, and the targeted population exhibited distinct characteristics. The participants received a briefing regarding the study’s purpose and were guaranteed confidentiality. The population taken into consideration for this study comprises male and female consumers aged 18 and above, who have been herbal cosmetic products users. This demographic is chosen because of their greater likelihood of engaging with herbal cosmetics and online platforms where eWOM communication occurs. The sampling frame will be derived from various sources, including digital platforms (social media) and online panel groups focused on beauty and cosmetics. This approach allows access to a large and diverse pool of potential participants who meet the study’s criteria, ensuring a robust and representative sample for the investigation. A sample of 482 online consumers was recruited. Taken after removing all outliers. The participants were required to have experienced online shopping and were exposed to eWOM. The survey was administered online, ensuring the anonymity and confidentiality of the responses. 3.2. Convergent validity and reliability Reliability refers to the consistency of measurement. Internal consistency, a crucial aspect of reliability, was evaluated via Cronbach’s alpha, a measure of how well the items within a scale correlate with each other (Nunnally, 1978) Values above 0.70 are generally considered acceptable, and the study’s reported alphas significantly exceeded this threshold, indicating excellent internal consistency: eWOM (α = 0.940), BI (α = 0.949), and PI (α = 0.902) (Figure 2). Composite reliability (Table 4), a more robust measure than Cronbach’s alpha, is particularly relevant in structural equation modeling and further substantiates the scales’ reliability. The reported values for rho_a eWOM: 0.945, BI: 0.949, PI: 0.905, and rho_c corroborated the high internal consistency. In Table 4, construct validity, which assesses the extent to which observed variables capture the underlying construct, was evaluated via average variance extracted (AVE). A higher AVE signifies greater convergent validity. The constructs used for this study demonstrated high AVE values. AVE values above 0.50 indicate that the construct explains more variance in its indicators than does error. The study’s AVE values for eWOM (0.551), BI (0.641), and PI (0.631) all surpassed this benchmark, demonstrating good convergent validity (Fornell & Larcker, 1981). Factor loading (Figure 2) is a measure of how much an observed variable correlates with the underlying latent construct. In short, it tells researchers how a particular variable is aligned with the factor, which provides insights into the relationships among the variables in a model. Development is generally considered significant when the load (+0.7) to the factor accounts for at least 49% of the variance (Hair et al., 2022). Such low loadings may be indicative of weak associations and thus may warrant closer scrutiny before inclusion in the final model. The results show that all the loadings are above the 0.7 threshold, which indicates a greater correlation between the observed variables. In conclusion, the high values of Cronbach’s alpha, the AVE, and composite reliability provide strong evidence for the reliability and convergent validity of the measured scales used in the research. Mediating analysis Mediating analysis is a research method used to explore how the relationship between two variables operates. It investigates whether the effect of an independent variable on a dependent variable is transmitted through an intermediate step (a mediator), shedding light on the underlying process or mechanism driving the connection (Baron and Kenny, 1986; Hayes, 2017). This approach helps researchers uncover not only whether a relationship exists but also how it unfolds by identifying the pathway through which the initial variable influences the outcome. For example, increased study time may improve exam scores primarily by increasing focus during learning, with focus acting as the mediator (Preacher and Hayes, 2008). Mediating analysis emphasizes understanding causal chains and the "why" behind observed effects, often employing statistical techniques such as bootstrapping to test indirect effects (Zhao et al., 2010). Table 8 below shows the results of the mediation analysis. H4: Brand image (BI) mediates the relationship between electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) and consumer purchase intention (PI). Table 8 presents the results of the mediation analysis that was performed to assess the mediating role of BI in the relationship between eWOM and PI (Hair et al., 2017). The overall total impact of eWOM on PI was significant (β=0.750, t=27.718, p=<0.001). With the inclusion of BI as a mediating variable, a significant indirect effect of eWOM and PI was found (β=0.491, t=7.835, p=<0.001). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Kothari and Mani (2026) 9 Table 8 Mediating analysis. Implications These findings offer valuable insights into the interplay between eWOM, BI, and PI within the digital marketplace while considering herbal cosmetic products. In existing studies, researchers have analyzed BI as a mediator in the connection between eWOM and PI. Smart PLS bootstrapping has been carried out to measure direct and indirect effects. The specific direct impact of the path coefficients between factors of eWOM-> PI (β=0.254, t=3.718, p=0.000) indicates a favorable relationship. Mediation is confirmed, as there is a direct effect of 0.259, an indirect effect of 0.491, and a total effect of 0.750 in the analysis, which indicates a positive mediation effect. Additionally, as expected, all p values are under the given threshold of <0.001 affirming the positive relationship between the variables eWOM, BI, and PI. The factors of herbal cosmetics for eWOM are significant, and BI has a significant effect on PI. The significant path coefficients indicate the strength and direction of the relationships, whereas the p values provide information about the statistical significance of the relationships. The confirmed hypotheses highlight the influence of eWOM on consumer behavior significantly. Specifically, the direct effect of eWOM on PI reinforces the importance of online consumer opinions in shaping buying decisions. Consumers rely strongly on online reviews and recommendations before they make purchases, showing the power of eWOM. Moreover, a partial mediation of BI shows that a more nuanced relationship is created. eWOM not only directly impacts the PI but also indirectly shapes it by influencing consumers’ perceptions of the brand. A favorable or positive BI, cultivated through favorable eWOM, can significantly increase the likelihood of consumers buying products or services. The results have substantial implications for marketing and brand management strategies in this digital era, which can be discussed (Figure 3): • eWOM Management Businesses should prioritize actively encouraging customer satisfaction and putting consumers first so that they would want to share their positive experiences online. Simultaneously, strategies for managing and responding to negative eWOM are crucial. Addressing negative reviews and resolving customer issues publicly can mitigate damage and demonstrate responsiveness for many brands. • Brand Building through eWOM Given the strong influence of eWOM on BI, companies should integrate eWOM into their brand-building initiatives. Leveraging positive and favorable consumer feedback to reinforce brand values and associations can strengthen brand perception and build customer loyalty and repurchase considerations. • Alignment of Online and Offline Brand Experiences The consistency between the BI projected through eWOM and the actual customer experience is paramount. Any discrepancy can erode trust and lead to negative and unfavorable eWOM. Ensuring a positive and consistent brand experience across all touchpoints, both online and offline, is essential for fostering positive word-of-mouth for brands. • eWOM Monitoring and Analysis The implementation of systems to analyze and track eWOM provides valuable data-driven insights into consumer perceptions or purchase intent, preferences, and potential areas for advancement. This information can improve product development, customer service strategies, and overall brand management. Understanding the nuances of online conversations surrounding a brand allows for more targeted and effective marketing efforts. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Kothari and Mani (2026) 10 Figure 3 Enhancing brand strategies through eWOM for customer engagement. 8. Conclusion Finally, this research confirmed that PI, as the dependent variable of the eWOM effect, strongly had a greater impact on the area of herbal cosmetic products. The overall results highlight the importance of managing online communications and utilizing them to establish robust brand images in the digital marketplace. According to the results, eWOM positively correlates with PI, with a strong path coefficient and statistical significance. BI acts as a vital intermediary, thereby explaining how eWOM impacts consumer purchasing decisions not only directly but also indirectly through forming an image of the brand to benefit the PI. The bottom line for marketers is that encouraging positive eWOM could be one of the most effective sales drivers in an online environment where consumers increasingly form their purchasing decisions from the information they read about brands and products in distant corners of the web. eWOM significantly influences consumer decision-making and enhances BI. This study implies that eWOM has a dual effect, both as a direct driver of PI and as a catalyst for enhancing BI, which in turn increases the likelihood of purchase. These results have important repercussions for marketers and enterprises that prefer their operations in the internet realm, particularly those that are involved in the herbal cosmetics production sector. Because of the substantial role that it plays in molding customers’ views of brands and encouraging consumers’ intentions to make purchases, the findings imply that businesses should make investments in initiatives that promote positive online reviews. Furthermore, marketers should recognize the importance of nurturing a favorable BI, as this could amplify the effectiveness of eWOM in influencing consumer behavior. In conclusion, this research sheds light on the entangled link that exists between eWOM, BI, and PI. It offers organizations important insights that can be used to harness digital word-of-mouth to increase revenue and promote customer engagement. The intricacies of eWOM in various product categories and its ever-changing influence on customer behavior in a digital ecosystem that is always developing might be further studied. 9. Future Research Directions The current study provides important insights into the relationships among eWOM, BI, and PI, but a few limitations should be acknowledged. These limitations offer avenues for future research to enhance understanding in this domain. • Cross-Sectional Design: The cross-sectional design of the study restricts the ability to establish definitive causal inferences. Future research can employ longitudinal designs that could better capture the dynamic interplay of eWOM, BI, and PI over time, allowing for stronger causal inferences. • General Online Consumer Focus: The emphasis on general online customers places bounds on the applicability of findings to specific product categories or industries. Future analyses could explore these relationships vertically (fashion, electronics, or travel) to determine whether industry differences exist and, thus, how to refine marketing strategies accordingly. Therefore, if sufficient data are available, searching for the niche market and specific customer segment can deliver valuable insights. • Variable scope: Future studies can encompass additional mediating or moderating variables, such as customer trust, product involvement, or perceived risk, to gain better insight into the association between eWOM and PI. Examining how educational factors or individual differences impact this could add depth to the analysis. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Kothari and Mani (2026) 11 • Study limitations: The self-reported method used to collect data in this study may be inherently limited. Future research could explore other methods of data collection across different product types, geographic locations, and industries to deepen the understanding of customer motivations and decision-making. By overcoming these limitations, a more nuanced understanding of the eWOM, BI, and PI associations in the digital market can contribute to future research. With this knowledge, businesses can double their marketing strategies and engage with customers in a way that strengthens brand relationships in the changing digital landscape. JSON: Name: ewom_brand_image_mediation Title: Partial least squares structural equation modeling of electronic word-of-mouth effects on consumer purchase intention in the herbal cosmetics market Short Hypothesis: Positive electronic word-of-mouth increases consumer purchase intention, and this effect is partially mediated by brand image. Related Work: Prior research has primarily quantified the relationship between electronic word-of-mouth, brand image, and purchase intention using cross-sectional survey data and structural equation modeling variants. Two dominant analytic strategies are covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) and variance-based PLS-SEM; both estimate latent constructs and path coefficients but differ in sample-size and distributional requirements. Alternative approaches include multiple regression and bootstrapped mediation tests to estimate direct and indirect effects, and recent studies augment self-report measures with automated sentiment analysis of online reviews. Reported limitations across existing work include heavy reliance on cross-sectional self-report questionnaires (raising common-method bias), narrow domain samples that restrict generalization, limited use of objective behavioral outcomes (actual purchases), inconsistent reporting of measurement quality (AVE/CR/HTMT), few head-to-head comparisons between CB-SEM and PLS-SEM, and scarce multi-group or longitudinal analyses to test stability of effects. Unresolved issues include the magnitude and stability of mediation by brand image across contexts, the role of omitted variables (trust, perceived risk), and external validity when moving from intention to observed purchase. Abstract: This research formalizes a reproducible pipeline to test whether electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) causally affects consumer purchase intention for herbal cosmetics, and whether brand image partially mediates that effect. The approach combines validated multi-item survey scales with structural equation modeling using PLS-SEM, supplemented by bootstrapped mediation tests and comparative analyses using CB-SEM and regression baselines. The main contribution is a concrete experimental workflow: measurement-model evaluation (factor loadings, AVE, CR, HTMT), model-fit assessment (SRMR, NFI), hypothesis testing (path coefficients, bootstrapped confidence intervals), and prespecified ablation studies (remove mediator, replace mediator with trust or perceived risk, compare PLS-SEM vs CB-SEM). Expected outcomes are precise estimates of direct, indirect, and total effects, quantified mediation strength (VAF), and evidence on whether eWOM influences intention beyond brand image. The pipeline supports reproducible assessment of construct validity and generalization across demographic subgroups and enables integration of self-report and behavioral review data to evaluate external validity. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary survey dataset: N_target=600 respondents who are herbal cosmetics users, quotas on age/gender/residence to approximate the target population; instrument: validated multi-item 5-point Likert scales for eWOM (15 items), Brand Image (12 items), Purchase Intention (7 items), plus controls (age, gender, income, prior purchase). (2) Secondary behavioral dataset: scraped reviews and ratings for herbal-cosmetics brands from two e-commerce platforms, N_reviews>=20,000 with metadata (rating, timestamp, brand, product). Baselines: (A) PLS-SEM (proposed pipeline); (B) CB-SEM using maximum-likelihood estimation; (C) OLS/multiple regression with composite scores; (D) mediation via Baron-Kenny regressions and bootstrapped indirect effect; (E) predictive classifier (logistic regression / random forest) predicting actual purchase from review-derived features and survey composites. Evaluation metrics: measurement: factor loadings, AVE, composite reliability (CR), Cronbach's alpha, HTMT; model fit: SRMR, NFI (PLS) and RMSEA, CFI, Chi-square (CB-SEM); hypothesis testing: standardized path coefficients, t-statistics, p-values, 95% bootstrap CIs (bootstrap resamples=5,000); explanatory power: R^2 for Purchase Intention; mediation strength: indirect effect and VAF; effect sizes: f^2; predictive metrics (behavioral): accuracy, precision, recall, AUC on 80/20 train/test split, with 5-fold CV for hyperparameter tuning. Experimental setup: data cleaning (missingness thresholds, listwise deletion if >20% missing, otherwise multiple imputation), outlier detection via Mahalanobis distance, test for multicollinearity (VIF<5), confirmatory factor analysis for CB-SEM, PLS-SEM measurement model assessment, structural model bootstrapping (5,000), multi-group analysis by gender and age cohorts (configural invariance tests), ablation studies: (i) remove Brand Image mediator and measure change in direct eWOM->PI path and R^2; (ii) replace Brand Image with Trust and with Perceived Risk and compare indirect effects and VAF; (iii) compare PLS-SEM vs CB-SEM parameter estimates and fit indices; (iv) combine survey composites with behavioral review-derived sentiment features to predict actual purchase and compare predictive performance versus survey-only models. Risk Factors and Limitations: Cross-sectional survey design limits causal inference and temporal ordering; self-reported purchase intention may not translate to actual purchase behavior; common-method variance due to single-source survey responses can inflate path estimates; sample selection and nonresponse bias may reduce external validity and overrepresent urban/young respondents; measurement model misspecification (poorly performing items) can bias latent estimates; multicollinearity among constructs (e.g., brand image and trust) can distort mediation estimates; PLS-SEM provides different parameterization than CB-SEM and may produce inconsistent estimates when distributional assumptions are violated; CB-SEM may be underpowered if sample <300 for complex models; scraped review data contains noise, bots, and platform-specific biases and may not map to surveyed individuals; linking behavioral and survey data may be infeasible due to privacy constraints; effect sizes may be small and sensitive to omitted confounders (e.g., price promotions, product availability); demographic and cultural limits constrain generalization beyond the studied market (herbal cosmetics in the sampled region).
